Inner Court
IN-er KORT
n. (the court nearest the house, the court of the priests)
Hebrew chatser ha-penimith, the inner court, from chatser, an enclosure or court, and panim, the face or inward part. Named nineteen times in the Authorized Version.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The inner court is the enclosure nearest the house of the LORD, divided from the outer court and reserved for the service of the altar. Solomon built it of hewn stone and cedar: “And he built the inner court with three rows of hewed stone, and a row of cedar beams” (1 Kings 6:36). It is where the brasen altar stood, and where the priests and Levites ministered; Ezekiel's vision measures its gates and its chambers in detail. The phrase also carries into the courts of kings, where the inner court was the place a man entered only when called — Esther risked her life to come in uncalled. Scripture uses the distinction between the courts to teach degrees of nearness. Israel came into the outer court; the priests served in the inner; the high priest alone passed within the veil, and that once a year with blood. The gradation was not snobbery but instruction: God is approachable, and He is approachable on His terms. The most terrible scene in Ezekiel happens here — “And he brought me into the inner court of the LORD'S house” (Ezekiel 8:16), and there in the holiest ground short of the sanctuary itself, five and twenty men had turned their backs on the temple to worship the rising sun. Nearness of place is not nearness of heart.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Inner court, the court next the house of the LORD, built of hewn stone and cedar, reserved for the priests and the altar; also the innermost court of a king's palace.

Hebrew chatser ha-penimith, the inner court.

From chatser, an enclosure, a court, and panim, the face, the inward part.

Built by Solomon with three rows of hewed stone and a row of cedar beams, 1 Kings 6:36.

Called also the court of the priests, 2 Chronicles 4:9.

Used also of the innermost court of a palace, Esther 4:11.

Key Scripture

1Ki 6:36 — "And he built the inner court with three rows of hewed stone, and a row of cedar beams."

Eze 8:16 — "And he brought me into the inner court of the LORD'S house, and, behold, at the door of the temple of the LORD, between the porch and the altar, were about five and twenty men, with their backs toward the temple of the LORD, and their faces toward the east; and they worshipped the sun toward the east."

Eze 10:3 — "Now the cherubims stood on the right side of the house, when the man went in; and the cloud filled the inner court."

Est 4:11 — "All the king's servants, and the people of the king's provinces, do know, that whosoever, whether man or woman, shall come unto the king into the inner court, who is not called, there is one law of his to put him to death, except such to whom the king shall hold out the golden sceptre, that he may live: but I have not been called to come in unto the king these thirty days."

Modern Corruption

Degrees of nearness to God are read as mere clericalism; Scripture uses the courts to teach that access is real and is on God's terms.

expand to see more

Two opposite errors meet at the inner court. The first is sacerdotal: the Roman and Anglo-Catholic reading takes the gradation of courts as permanent, and builds a priesthood that stands between the people and God in the new covenant as the sons of Aaron did in the old. The epistle to the Hebrews is written against precisely this, and the rent veil answers it. The second error is the modern evangelical flattening, which treats all distinctions of holiness as pretension, and so loses the fear of God along with the fences.

The dictionary holds the Reformed and Baptist position: the courts were real and the gradation was God's, and it has been fulfilled, not abolished by sentiment. Every believer is now a priest with access into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, which is a greater nearness than the inner court ever gave to any Levite. But Ezekiel 8 stands as the warning that attends it. Those men were standing in the inner court, as near as a layman could get, with their backs to the house. Privilege of position is not piety, and it never was.
